title: Strings
description: String immutability, comparison, common methods, and the StringBuilder/StringBuffer alternative for building text.
objectives: Compare strings correctly with equals() vs ==
Know when to use StringBuilder instead of String concatenation

content.heading: Immutability and Comparison
content.body: A Java String is immutable — once created, its contents never change; every 'modifying' method (like replace() or toUpperCase()) returns a brand-new String rather than altering the original. String literals are interned (pooled): two literal Strings with the same text, like "cat" and "cat", typically refer to the exact same object in the string pool, which is why == can appear to 'work' for literals — but this is an unreliable implementation detail, not a guarantee, especially once Strings are built at runtime (via concatenation, new String(...), or user input). The correct, reliable way to compare String content is always .equals() (or .equalsIgnoreCase() for case-insensitive comparison).

content.heading: Common Methods and StringBuilder
content.body:
Useful String methods: length() (a method here, unlike array's .length field), charAt(i) (the character at index i), substring(begin, end) (characters from begin up to, excluding, end), indexOf(sub) (position of the first occurrence, or -1), split(regex) (breaks the string into an array around a pattern), and replace(old, new).

Because String is immutable, repeatedly concatenating in a loop with + creates a new String object every single time, which is inefficient for many concatenations. StringBuilder (or the older, thread-safe StringBuffer) provides a mutable sequence of characters: sb.append(x) modifies the same underlying buffer in place, and sb.toString() converts to a final String only once, at the end — the standard, efficient pattern for building up a string piece by piece.

content.explanation: new String("cat") deliberately creates a distinct object from the literal, demonstrating why == is unreliable for String comparison. StringBuilder builds the result in one mutable buffer instead of creating five separate intermediate String objects.

keyPoints: String is immutable — every transformation returns a new String
Always use .equals() (not ==) to compare String content
length() is a method on String, unlike the .length field on arrays
Use StringBuilder for repeated concatenation instead of + in a loop
commonMistakes: Confusing String's .length() method with an array's .length field
Concatenating strings with + inside a large loop instead of using StringBuilder
